by: session, 20 Oct 2026: Adrian's second notes — question now y = 2e^{-3x} + 1 (the minus effect and the shift up), labels inside the corner box, note under the 2, the asymptote explained on the board

beats.say: First, the four basic shapes of exponential graphs. Most importantly, learn each shape, and which axis it is flipped in.
asks: Why learn the four shapes?

beats.say: Y equals E to the X: the basic shape. It grows faster and faster, and stays above the X axis.
asks: Why does it grow faster and faster?
Why is it always above the x-axis?

beats.say: Y equals E to the power minus X: a minus in front of X flips it in the Y axis.
asks: Why does a minus in front of x flip it in the y-axis?

beats.say: Y equals minus E to the X: a minus in front of the graph flips it in the X axis.
asks: Why does a minus in front flip it downwards?

beats.say: Y equals minus E to the power minus X: both minuses, so it is flipped twice, in both axes.
asks: How do I know which of the four shapes to use?

beats.say: Now sketch Y equals two E to the power minus three X, plus one. Start with empty axes at the side.
asks: Why start with empty axes?

beats.say: Three steps: first the shape, then shift it up, and last the intercepts. We draw the graph as we go.
asks: Why these three steps?
Why find the shape first?

beats.say: Step one, the shape. It is the minus sign that matters. Here the minus is in front of X.
asks: Where else could a minus sign be?

beats.say: So it has the shape of E to the power minus X, from the corner. Lift it onto the axes.
asks: Why the shape of e to the power minus x?

beats.say: The two and the three do not change the shape. They only stretch it. Only a minus sign would flip it.
asks: What do the 2 and the 3 do then?

beats.say: Step two, shift it up. As X grows, two E to the power minus three X gets closer and closer to zero.
asks: Why does it get closer to zero?
What happens when x is negative?

beats.say: Try some values. When X is one, it is about zero point one. When X is two, about zero point zero zero five.
asks: Why does it get smaller as x grows?
Will it ever reach zero?

beats.say: Without the plus one, the asymptote would be Y equals zero. With it, Y gets closer to zero plus one, which is one.
asks: Why do we add the 1?

beats.say: Plus one shifts the whole graph up by one unit. The asymptote moves up from Y equals zero to Y equals one.
asks: Does the shape change when we shift?
Why does the asymptote move too?

beats.say: Step three, the intercepts. For the Y intercept, sub X equals zero into the full equation.
asks: Why the full equation, with the plus one?

beats.say: Y equals two E to the power negative three times zero, plus one.
asks: Why do we put 0 into the power?

beats.say: Negative three times zero is zero, so we get two E to the power zero, plus one.
asks: Why is negative three times zero zero?

beats.say: E to the power zero is one. So Y equals two times one, plus one, which is three.
asks: Why is e to the power 0 one?

beats.say: For the X intercept, sub Y equals zero into the full equation.
asks: Why put y = 0 for the x-intercept?

beats.say: Then solve for E to the power minus three X. It equals negative one half.
asks: How do we get negative one half?

beats.say: But E to any power is always positive, never negative. So there are no solutions, and no X intercept.
asks: Does no solutions mean I made a mistake?

do.text: e to a power is always positive

read: A positive number to any power is still positive.
It can never equal $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, or any negative number.
**So $e^{-3x} = -\tfrac{1}{2}$ has no solutions: the curve never meets the $x$-axis.**

beats.say: So the sketch has the shape of E to the power minus X, through zero, three, above the asymptote Y equals one.
asks: Do I need to label the asymptote?
Why is there no x-intercept on the sketch?
